newsitem.title: UK: Dollar loses froth in late Europe but still sparky.
newsitem.headline: Dollar loses froth in late Europe but still sparky.

text.p: The dollar was firm but off peaks in late Europe after storming up on the back of German and U.S. comments on its status in the run-up to EU monetary union.

A degree of calm settled on the U.S. unit, which hit 23-month peaks against the mark and Swiss franc after Bundesbank member Otmar Issing predicted a shift from marks to dollars and New York Federal Reserve Bank President William McDonough said the dollar would become more important as EMU approached.
"There's clearly still a G3 commitment to a stronger dollar," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International in London.
"We've had a three-pfennig rise -- that's quite a move for one day so the market's taking stock after that. But clearly underlying sentiment towards the dollar is positive," he said.
The dollar was quoted at 1.5662/72 marks at 1602 GMT, down from its high of 1.5735 but still well up from late Monday's European level of 1.5445/50.

Figures showing German industrial output fell 1.8 percent in October from the previous month supported dollar/mark as they highlighted Germany's economic difficulties and revived speculation of a reduction in German interest rates. But the Bundesbank moved to dampen easing expectations.

A spokesman questioned by Reuters declined to comment directly on the talk but pointed to earlier comments by Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer that there was "no short-term reason" for an interest rate change.
"(The industrial production data) suggest that the strength of the mark against the yen is causing problems for exporters," said Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident here.
But "as Tietmeyer has hinted it will be some while yet before the Bundesbank is convinced of the need for a further interest rate cut," he added.
Mark/yen lurched downhill during the session.
The mark slid to 72.57/60 yen by 1631 GMT from 73.78/81 in late Europe on Monday. It was also down on European crosses.

"In Germany, we are looking at what can be termed a bumpy recovery at best," said Jeremy Stretch, currency strategist at NatWest Markets in London. "The economic outlook should keep the mark soft against the dollar and its European crosses."
The dollar pushed to 23-month highs against the Swiss and French francs overnight, before retreating slightly in European dealings, but softened against the yen.
The dollar pushed to an intraday high of 114.60 yen but had eased to 113.65/70 by 1632 GMT from Monday's close of 113.90/95.

Sterling had a rollercoaster day. It surged to 2.6370 marks overnight, its best level since crashing out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism in September 1992, but fell all the way back to 2.5745/55 by 1642 GMT -- more than two pfennings down from late Monday's level here of 2.5972/82.
Traders said the current volatility made the market almost impossible to read and perilous to play.
"It's coming to the end of the year, people have got bonuses to worry about -- I'm certainly not going home with a position," said one.
